newsitem.title: INDIA: Reports fishermen escaped cyclone - Indian officials.
newsitem.headline: Reports fishermen escaped cyclone - Indian officials.

text.p: Authorities in India's cyclone-ravaged southern Andhra Pradesh state on Tuesday said they had reports that some fishermen, presumed missing or dead in last week's storm, had reached safety.
"We are trying to verify reports that some of them had returned to safety but far away from their villages," said a spokesman for the state government.

Officials had earlier said that about 1,300 fishermen were missing from the coastal villages of East Godavari and West Godavari districts. Hopes of finding them alive had been fading after air and seas searches failed to sight their boats.
A state government spokesman said on Monday the maximum expected death toll from the cyclone was 2,000 if fears that the fishermen had perished proved correct.

There were local reports that some of the fishing boats which set sail one or two days before the cyclone struck had made land about 50 kilometres to 100 kilometres south of Amalapuram in East Godavari.
At Etimoga village near the port town of Kakinada, the district headquarters of East Godavari, women and children waited in the hope that some 778 relatives had survived the cyclone and would return.
State chief minister Chandrababu Naidu told a gathering at the village that helicopters and the coast guard were making every effort to locate their missing men.
But the assurance had little effect on the crowd.
Malladi Dhanalaxi, 40, whose four brothers were among the missing, wept inconsolably.
"I don't think they will ever come back," she wailed.
Six days after the cyclone, the once-prosperous region was still reeling from the disaster which Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda described as a national calamity.

Relief camps are sheltering 179,000 people whose homes have been destroyed or badly damaged, and medical teams are treating the injured, mostly for broken bones, and inoculating the evacuees against waterborne diseases such as cholera.
Officials said on Tuesday that so far no cases of cholera had been reported.
Gowda has called a meeting of officials of federal and state governments, banks and relief agencies for Wednesday to discuss ways and means of helping the cyclone victims.
State officials said a detailed assessment of the number of deaths, crop and livestock losses and damage to property would also be completed by Wednesday.
The latest estimate on losses to crops and property was 53.75 billion rupees ($1.5 billion).
The two affected districts grow paddy (rice) besides the cash crops of coconut, sugarcane, cashewnut and banana.
Officials said nearly four million people out of a 10 million population in the two districts had been affected by the cyclone which many survivors said had been the most severe in memory.
Officials claimed that relief supplies, including rice, kerosene and cash, had reached almost all villages except a few which were still inaccessible.
They said helicopters air-dropped food packets and water bottles to survivors in the villages that could not be reached.
